summary:
A trans visitor to Montana stands under the United States national travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Montana has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the Montana Constitution, and Montana is the only state to improve in the 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment rankings. Adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect as a result of that court record.

On 24 March 2026 Montana enacted Senate Bill 437, defining sex as a binary of male or female based on primary sexual anatomy and reproductive system (female as ova-based, male as sperm-based), defining man, woman, mother and father on that basis, and providing that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role. The definitions apply in more than 60 sections of state law, including driver's licenses, marriage licenses and anti-discrimination protections, and applicants for driver's and marriage licenses must list sex as so defined. Plaintiffs sought in April 2026 to add SB 437 to ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to Senate Bill 458, which had been struck down in February 2025 by District Judge Leslie Halligan for violating the equal protection clauses of the Montana Constitution.

Identity-document changes remain contested. Montana's 2022 health department rule barring gender-identity-based changes to birth-certificate sex, the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate to change driver's-license sex, and portions of 2023 Senate Bill 458 were preliminarily enjoined in December 2024 by a Helena district court, which found plaintiffs likely to succeed on claims that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination violating the Montana Constitution's fundamental right to be free from sex discrimination. That preliminary block was upheld on 15 April 2026 by the Montana Supreme Court, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. Litigation over these document rules continues.

Facilities rules are also contested. In February 2025 the Montana legislature passed HB 121, requiring bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly-funded facilities to be segregated based on biological sex assigned at birth. The ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta temporarily restrained enforcement, ruling that the law is motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A December 2024 Montana House proposal to forbid trans people from using Capitol bathrooms was voted down.

Gender-affirming care for trans minors was banned by Senate Bill 99, signed 28 April 2023 by Governor Greg Gianforte and described as the most comprehensive prohibition in the United States. It was preliminarily enjoined on 27 September 2023 by District Judge Jason Marks, kept in place on 11 December 2024 by the Montana Supreme Court on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and permanently struck down on 14 May 2025 by Judge Marks for failure to clearly and convincingly establish a bona fide health risk. Gender-affirming care for minors therefore remains lawful in Montana, though federal policy shifts and litigation keep the youth-side picture unstable nationally.

Montana's hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act signed in October 2009. Federal Title VII protections for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County (decided 15 June 2020) apply in Montana, and by executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules, broadened in November 2008 by Executive Order 41-2008, and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016. Ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with Missoula County covering county employees only.

In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed religious-belief legislation granting the right to discriminate if religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as allowing a license to discriminate against LGBTQ people. In May 2023 HB 359 prohibited sexually oriented or obscene performances in public spaces where minors may be present and explicitly prohibited drag story hours at publicly-funded schools and libraries, leading a Butte-Silver Bow library to cancel a transgender woman's reading; District Judge Brian Morris issued a temporary restraining order in July 2023, extended October 2024, blocking enforcement as vague and overbroad with risk of disproportionate enforcement against trans, Two-Spirit, and gender nonconforming people. A March 2025 bill, HB 675, defining drag as inherently sexual was defeated with 13 Republicans joining Democrats.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined enforcement of the state ban effective immediately, and mooted by Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015. Montana permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, with Kulstad v. Maniaci affirmed 6-1 on 7 October 2009. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has their marriage and partnership recognized in Montana.

An April 2021 law banning transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.
tangentialFactors:
Montana's trajectory diverges from the national pattern. While many states have moved to restrict trans rights without effective judicial check, Montana's courts have repeatedly intervened under the state constitution, making it the only state to improve in the 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment rankings. This does not mean the legislature has stopped legislating: Senate Bill 437 was enacted in March 2026, and litigation over it is pending.

The federal layer above Montana remains the sharper risk for a visitor. Passport marker restrictions, entry-screening measures and executive-order-driven facility bans apply regardless of how Montana's courts rule, so a favourable state court record does not neutralise federal document and entry exposure.

Montana's pattern of judicial restraint on adult restrictions contrasts with states where such laws are in force, but the youth-side picture nationally is unstable because of federal policy shifts and ongoing litigation, so care-access expectations should be verified close to travel.

HB 819, signed in May 2025 with immediate effect, prohibits flags representing political party, race, sexual orientation, gender or political ideology on government property and public schools, thereby banning Pride and other LGBTQ flags, while permitting official historical flags including the Gadsden flag, law-enforcement/Thin Blue Line flags, tribal nation, foreign country, military service branch, POW/MIA, and official school or government entity flags. This is a symbolic measure rather than a direct restriction on a trans visitor, but it signals the legislative climate.
localsOnly:
Montana residents can change gender markers on identity documents under rules that have shifted repeatedly and remain subject to litigation. Prior rules required sex reassignment surgery and clinical treatment until December 2017, when the surgery requirement was removed in favour of a Correction Affidavit, Gender Designation Form and court order plus doctor letter for licenses; an April 2021 law reintroducing surgical procedures and a court order was blocked in April 2022 for lack of clear legal definitions, after which the Department imposed a temporary emergency rule in May 2022 banning updates, made permanent months later. The December 2024 preliminary injunction and its April 2026 affirmance currently govern, pausing enforcement of the 2022 rule and related restrictions while litigation continues.

By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules by Governor Marc Racicot, broadened in November 2008 by Governor Brian Schweitzer's Executive Order 41-2008, and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016 by Governor Steve Bullock. Federal Title VII protections for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County apply, and local ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish add coverage in employment, housing and public accommodations.

Montana hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed religious-belief legislation granting the right to discriminate if religious beliefs are substantially burdened.

Gender-affirming care for trans minors is not banned following the permanent striking down of SB 99 on 14 May 2025, though federal measures affecting minors' care remain in flux nationally.

A 2018 Montana Family Foundation initiative to require public bathroom use corresponding to birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures for the November ballot, and a December 3, 2024 Montana House proposal to forbid trans people from using Capitol bathrooms was voted down. HB 121, passed February 2025, is temporarily restrained as of 2 April 2025.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997 (Gryczan v. State), with the enjoined sodomy provision legislatively repealed on 18 April 2013. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since 19 November 2014, and Montana Supreme Court recognized common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019. Montana permits adoption with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, with Kulstad v. Maniaci affirmed 6-1 on 7 October 2009; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilization with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized if married, and surrogacy is unregulated with courts generally favourable.

In May 2025 HB 819, a flag-neutrality law, prohibited official government display of flags representing sexual orientation, interpreted to prohibit Pride flags; Missoula adopted a rainbow pride flag as its municipal flag, effectively exempting it statewide. A May 2021 parental opt-in law requires parental consent before K-12 sex education.
outOfScopeNotes:
The operative status of Senate Bill 437 is unresolved: it was enacted 24 March 2026 and plaintiffs sought in April 2026 to add it to ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to SB 458, but no source in this inventory records a ruling on SB 437 itself. Whether its definitions are currently enforced in driver's-license and marriage-license practice is not sourced here.

The scope of the December 2024 preliminary injunction, as affirmed April 2026, over the 2022 health department rule and Motor Vehicle Division policy is described as pausing enforcement "while litigation continues," but the inventory does not state whether final judgment has since been entered or whether any narrow categories of document change are currently permitted.

HB 121's temporary restraining order of 2 April 2025 is recorded, but whether it has since been converted to a preliminary injunction, dissolved, or upheld on appeal is not sourced in this inventory.

The inventory does not address how Montana's document rules interact with federal passport processing under Executive Order 14168 for a visitor presenting inconsistent state and federal markers; that interaction is not sourced here.

Whether Montana has any state-level analogue to federal entry-screening or visa-flagging measures is not addressed in the inventory.

The current enforcement posture of HB 359 following the July 2023 temporary restraining order extended October 2024 is not resolved in this inventory; no final ruling is recorded.
